newsitem.title: UK: Charity opposes military intervention in Zaire.
newsitem.headline: Charity opposes military intervention in Zaire.

text.p: A British-based charity warned on Thursday against military intervention by Western countries in the fighting in eastern Zaire and said involvement by France in particular could exacerbate the problem.
"Military intervention is not the answer in Zaire. It will take too long and, even if agreed, may well compound the problems in the region," the Save the Children Fund said in a statement.
The priority was to restore stability, it added, and that required support for hundreds of thousands of local people displaced or otherwise affected by the fighting in the area.
Save the Children said it also required help with the "major and rapid voluntary repatriation" of Rwandan refugees.
Mark Bowden, the charity's east Africa director who has just returned from a meeting with field workers in the region, said military protection was not necessary for the aid effort.
"Given that journalists have been there in Goma...we have no reason to believe that certain areas are inaccessible," he said.

European Union aid ministers were meeting on Thursday to discuss the crisis. France and Spain have said they could send troops to the area, perhaps as part of a force to open safe corridors to facilitate food deliveries.

However, French forces based in eastern Zaire intervened in western Rwanda in 1994, setting up safe havens for refugees, most of them Hutus who were fleeing civil war and reprisals for the Hutu genocide of up to one million Tutsis and Hutu moderates.
Bowden said French involvement meant any EU intervention "will be seen as a partisan force".
"Frankly, the French will be unacceptable in the region. In a sense they are seen as being responsible for the present situation," he said.
Bowden said Save the Children wanted the EU to support a monitoring group along the border between Zaire and Rwanda to help prevent incursions by the Rwandan army into Zaire.
The charity wanted action to encourage the voluntary repatriation of "innocent refugees" back to Rwanda.

Bowden said aid offered in transit centres in eastern Zaire would give Rwandans an incentive to move back towards their country. Armed militants had made the camps where Hutus settled after fleeing Rwanda in 1994 highly dangerous for aid workers.
The EU should also help the returning refugees in their home villages until they were able to support themselves, he said.
